items.prose: A lottery picks one of 64 equally likely numbers.
items.question: What is the surprise of the winning number, in bits?

feedback.generic: Not quite. How many halvings take 64 down to 1?

byKey.count: You gave the count. The surprise is its base 2 log.

explain.text: $64 = 2^6$, so six yes or no questions pick the number: 6 bits.

items.prose: A signal is long, flat or short with chances 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2.
items.question: What is its entropy, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh each surprise by its chance.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the surprises 1, 1.737 and 2.322 equally.

explain.text: The surprises are 1, 1.737 and 2.322 bits. Weighted by 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 they add to 1.485 bits.

items.prose: A code uses the words 0, 10, 11 and 110.
items.question: Is it a prefix code?

options.text: Yes: the words are all different
options.why: Different words are not enough. A whole word must not start another.
10 starts with 1, not 0. Look at 11 and 110.

feedback.correct: 11 is the start of 110, so the stream 110 is ambiguous.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each word against the longer ones.

explain.text: After reading 11 the receiver cannot tell whether a word has ended or 110 is coming. So it is not a prefix code.

items.prose: Huffman's method is run on chances 0.45, 0.25, 0.2 and 0.1. Its merges are 0.3, then 0.55, then 1.
items.question: What is the average length of the code, in bits? Give a decimal to 2 places.

widget.label: Average length
widget.accept: 1.85, the sum of the merged weights.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The average equals the sum of the merged weights, or $\sum p \ell$.

byKey.fixed: That is a fixed two-bit code.
byKey.entropy: That is the entropy, the floor.

explain.text: The lengths are 1, 2, 3 and 3, so $0.45 + 0.5 + 0.6 + 0.3 = 1.85$. Each merge adds one bit to every symbol beneath it. That is why the merged weights add to the same 1.85.

items.prose: Two fair dice are rolled independently.
items.question: What is the surprise of a double six, in bits? Give a decimal to 2 places.

byKey.one-die: That is one die. Two independent sixes add their surprises.
byKey.multiplied: You multiplied the surprises. They add.

items.prose: A prefix code has five words of lengths 1, 3, 3, 3 and 3.
items.question: What is its Kraft sum $\sum 2^{-\ell}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add $2^{-\ell}$ for each word.

byKey.lengths: You added the lengths. The budget adds $2^{-\ell}$.
byKey.half: That is the first word only.
byKey.one-each: You counted one word of length 3. There are four.

explain.text: The word of length 1 uses half the tree and each word of length 3 an eighth: $\tfrac12 + \tfrac48 = 1$. No word can be added without lengthening another.

items.prose: Three forecasts for a share each give chances to up, flat and down.
items.question: Which has the largest entropy?

options.why: One outcome takes 60%, so it is more predictable than a flatter split.
This is a fair coin, 1 bit. The flatter three-way split carries more.
One outcome takes 80%: this is the most predictable of the four.

feedback.correct: The flattest split, close to $\tfrac13$ each, carries the most.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The entropy is largest near equal chances.

explain.text: Entropy peaks at equal chances, $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits here. 0.35, 0.3, 0.35 is closest to equal.

items.prose: A text of 50,000 symbols has symbol counts whose entropy is 3.2 bits per symbol.
items.question: What is the fewest bytes a code built on those counts can use, on average? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply, then divide by 8.

byKey.bits: That is in bits. Divide by 8 for bytes.
byKey.symbols: That is one byte per symbol, the raw size.

explain.text: The entropy is the floor per symbol: $50{,}000 \times 3.2 / 8 = 20{,}000$ bytes.

items.prose: A coin is weighted 0.6 heads and 0.4 tails. The model also lists "lands on edge" with chance 0.
items.question: What is the entropy of the three outcomes, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.correct: The edge adds 0, so the entropy is that of 0.6 and 0.4: 0.971 bits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A chance of 0 adds nothing.

explain.text: $0.6 \times 0.737 + 0.4 \times 1.322 = 0.442 + 0.529 = 0.971$ bits, and the edge term $0 \log_2 0$ is taken as 0.

items.prose: A colleague's code for the weather averages 1.5 bits a report. The weather's entropy is 1.75 bits.
items.question: What must be true of the colleague's code?

options.text: It is not a prefix code, so some streams cannot be decoded
It is better than Huffman's code
options.why: No prefix code averages below the entropy, so this is no decodable code.

options.text: It is fine: the entropy is only an estimate
options.why: The chances are given, so the entropy is exact: 1.75 bits.

feedback.correct: An average below the entropy means the code cannot be decoded.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does the entropy bound say about prefix codes?

explain.text: Every prefix code averages at least the entropy. A shorter average is bought by words that start other words, so some streams have two readings.
